title: A World Full of Violence and a Man Who Found Favor
summary: The sons of God take wives from the daughters of men, the Nephilim appear, and human wickedness grows until every inclination of the human heart is evil. The LORD is grieved that he made humanity and resolves to blot it out. But Noah, a righteous man who walks with God, finds favor. God tells him to build an ark, promises to establish a covenant with him, and commands him to bring his family and pairs of every creature aboard, and Noah does everything God commands.
story: The genealogy of chapter 5 brought us to Noah and his father's hope that he would bring comfort from the curse. Chapter 6 shows how badly that comfort is needed. The violence that began with Cain and grew in Lamech has now filled the earth. The chapter is the turning point of the early history in Genesis: the world God called very good in chapter 1 is now, in God's own sight, corrupt. God's answer is judgment and rescue at the same time. He will undo the world by water, but he will carry a remnant through it and make a new start. The ark, the covenant, and Noah's obedience set up the flood narrative of chapters 7 and 8.
historical:
Stories of a great flood that destroyed early humanity were widespread in the ancient Near East. The Sumerian flood story, the Babylonian Atrahasis epic, and the eleventh tablet of the Epic of Gilgamesh all tell of the gods deciding to wipe out humanity, of one man warned in advance who builds a great boat, and of his survival along with animals. In Atrahasis the gods send the flood because humans have grown too many and too noisy and are disturbing their rest. In Genesis the reason is moral: violence and corruption. The flood hero in the Mesopotamian stories is saved because a friendly god breaks ranks and warns him; Noah is saved because the one God, who is also the judge, shows him favor. The similarities show that Genesis speaks into a shared memory; the differences show what it wants to say about God.

The ark's size, 300 by 50 by 30 cubits, comes to roughly 450 by 75 by 45 feet (about 137 by 23 by 14 meters), using the common cubit of about 18 inches, the length from elbow to fingertip. It is a vast rectangular barge, built to float rather than to sail, with three decks, a roof, and one door. The Gilgamesh epic describes its boat as a cube. The wood (gopher) is mentioned nowhere else and cannot be identified with certainty; cypress is a common suggestion.
cultural:
Verses 1 to 4 draw on ideas that ancient readers would have recognized and modern readers find strange. In the wider ancient world, kings and heroes were often said to be descended from gods, and stories of divine beings mating with humans were common. The Nephilim appear again in Numbers 13:33, when the Israelite spies claim to have seen them in Canaan, and the ancient Greek translation rendered the word giants. The mighty men of old, men of renown, sound like the legendary heroes of other nations' epics. Genesis mentions them briefly and without admiration; their fame is part of the problem, not the solution.

The instructions for the ark would have made sense to people who lived by rivers and knew how boats were made watertight. Pitch, a tar or bitumen, was used in Mesopotamia to waterproof boats and buildings, and a similar coating of tar and pitch seals the basket of the infant Moses (Exodus 2:3). The Hebrew word for ark, tevah, appears in only one other place in the Bible, as the name of that basket. Both are boxes that carry a chosen person through deadly water.
literary: The chapter has two halves joined by a new heading. Verses 1 to 8 close the section that began in 2:4 and end with a contrast: God sees that human wickedness is great, but Noah finds favor in the eyes of the LORD. (In Hebrew, the name Noah and the word favor use the same two letters in reverse order.) Verse 9 then opens This is the account of Noah, and the style changes to careful, repeated instruction. The key verb of the chapter is shachat, to ruin or corrupt. The earth was corrupt, all flesh had corrupted its way, and God says he will destroy it, using the same verb. The judgment matches the crime: God will finish the ruin that people had already begun. The chapter closes on a note of simple obedience that will return in the flood story: “So Noah did everything precisely as God had commanded him” (verse 22).

outline.t: The sons of God, the daughters of men, and the Nephilim
The LORD grieves over human wickedness; Noah finds favor
Noah the righteous in a corrupt and violent world
God tells Noah to build an ark
The coming flood, the promised covenant, and Noah's obedience

doctrines.note: Verse 5 is one of the Bible's most sweeping descriptions of the human condition: every inclination of the thoughts of the heart is evil all the time. Sin is not only a matter of deeds but of the heart's direction. Later Jewish teaching built its idea of the evil inclination on this verse, and Christian teaching on original sin draws on it too.

God's judgment in the flood is not arbitrary. It responds to violence that has filled the earth, and it matches what humanity has already done, since the same verb describes their corruption and his destruction. Judgment is God giving a ruined world over to the ruin it chose.

The LORD regretted that he had made man and was grieved in his heart. Scripture elsewhere says that God does not change his mind as humans do (Numbers 23:19; 1 Samuel 15:29), and theologians have understood language like this as God's real response to human evil described in human terms. God is not detached from the world. Sin grieves him.

Verse 18 contains the Bible's first use of the word covenant. Before the flood begins, God commits himself to Noah, promising a relationship that will carry him through judgment. The covenant is spelled out after the flood, in chapter 9.

words.note: Shachat, to ruin, spoil, or destroy. It is used in verses 11 and 12 for the earth's corruption and in verses 13 and 17 for God's destruction of it. The repetition makes a point: the flood is not God wrecking a healthy world, but God bringing to its end a world people had already ruined.

Chamas, violence. It means more than physical force; it covers injustice, bloodshed, and the abuse of power, especially by the strong against the weak. The prophets use it for oppression in Israel's own cities. In Genesis 6 it names the specific evil that filled the earth.

Tevah, ark or box. Apart from this story, it appears only for the basket in which the infant Moses was placed in the Nile (Exodus 2:3-5). It is a different word from the ark of the covenant. Both uses picture God preserving a chosen life through the waters of death.

Berit, covenant. A covenant was a binding agreement that formed a relationship with obligations and promises, often sealed by an oath or ritual. This is the word's first appearance in the Bible, and it will become one of Scripture's central ideas, running through Noah, Abraham, Sinai, David, and the new covenant.

christ: Jesus used the days of Noah as a picture of how his return will find the world: “As it was in the days of Noah, so will it be at the coming of the Son of Man” (Matthew 24:37). People were eating, drinking, and marrying, going on as usual until the flood came (Matthew 24:38-39; Luke 17:26-27). The warning is about being unready, not about the particular sins of Noah's generation. Hebrews 11:7 holds up Noah as a man of faith who built the ark in reverent fear, and Peter calls him “a preacher of righteousness” (2 Peter 2:5). Peter also sees in the ark a picture of salvation: “In the ark a few people, only eight souls, were saved through water” (1 Peter 3:20), a pattern he connects with baptism and with the resurrection of Christ. The link is typological, a pattern of rescue through judgment that the New Testament sees fulfilled in Christ, rather than a prediction in Genesis 6 itself.

hard.q: Who were the sons of God and the Nephilim?
hard.a:
This short passage has been read in three main ways. The oldest interpretation, found in Jewish writings such as 1 Enoch from the last centuries BC, takes the sons of God as angels or heavenly beings who crossed a boundary God had set and fathered children with human women. Supporters note that sons of God elsewhere in the Old Testament means heavenly beings (Job 1:6), and many think Jude 6 and 2 Peter 2:4, which speak of angels who sinned and abandoned their proper dwelling, allude to this story. A second view, made influential by Augustine and followed by many later Christian interpreters, takes the sons of God as the godly line of Seth and the daughters of men as the line of Cain, so that the sin is faithful people intermarrying with the ungodly. A third view, found among some ancient rabbis and modern scholars, sees the sons of God as powerful rulers who claimed divine status and took as many women as they pleased.

Each reading has difficulties. The first raises questions about angels and bodies, since Jesus says the angels do not marry. The second must explain why the text would use sons of God for one human line and men for another. The third has few clear parallels in biblical usage. Whatever the precise meaning, the passage shows boundaries being crossed and human pride swelling, and it explains why God sets a limit (verse 3) and why the flood follows.

questions: God sees that the earth is full of violence. Where do you see violence and the abuse of power in your own world, and how do you think God responds to it?
Noah is called righteous and blameless in his generation, living differently from everyone around him. What makes it hard to walk with God when your surroundings pull the other way?
The text says God was grieved in his heart. How does it affect your picture of God to know that human evil causes him grief and not only anger?
